doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Accompanying singers: Betty Carter, Krall and Connick
summary: Playing behind vocalists demands knowing the changes and supporting the singer; Betty was like a sax player; his rule is to play the right thing.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Was there a distinction playing behind a vocalist, like Betty Carter? Did she require something different than Elvin Jones did?

In general, yeah. Vocalists do. I mean it’s funny, Betty Carter was such a unique vocalist, I always conceptualized her as a sax player kind of, in a way. When I thought about her like that it made more sense to me. She was great, man. She was so challenging. Because she had a lot of different forms and speeds and a lot of it was kind of cues to the next section and they’d be different every night. So in that respect it wasn’t the usual just play a standard kind of singer. But yeah, I mean I played with Diana Krall and I played with Harry Connick and when you play standards with singers you have to really play the right notes. You have to really know the changes. And you have to be really aware of what you’re playing and how it affects the singer, and not get in their way, and be supportive. You know if I’m playing a standard with a tenor player you can fudge, you can play some different things you know. But you have to be really much more in tune and you have to play the right changes. It’s different. It’s a little harder I think.
Do you have a thought method that kicks in if you have to play “There Will Never Be Another You” in A flat instead of E flat?

I mean you know what? No matter if it’s a singer or whatever situation it is, whatever song, whatever key, whether it’s Elvin Jones or Diana Krall, I just try to play the right thing. I mean it’s really actually simple. I mean it’s really hard but there’s always a right thing to play. That’s what a lot of rhythm section people, it’s like there’s an obvious thing to play that feels right at that time, and that’s appropriate, whatever the situation may be. I always just try to find that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
